title: Steady wisdom
hookLine: one not shaken by sorrow nor craving joy is called steady in wisdom (Bhagavad Gita 2.56)
tomorrow: rivers pour in all day. why doesn't the ocean overflow?

cards: Hard news lands in the middle of dinner. One person at the table reads it, sets the phone face down, and keeps listening to the story someone was telling. Everyone notices.
That's yesterday's question, and Arjuna asks it outright. In the Gita he says to Krishna: the one steady in wisdom, how do they speak? How do they sit?
How do they walk? He is standing between two armies, and he doesn't want a theory. He wants to know how such a person moves through a day.

teach.b: Arjuna asks a practical question, and Krishna answers with a portrait of what happens inside. The walking follows from that.
The one whose mind isn't shaken by sorrow, who doesn't crave joy, who is free of clinging, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom. In Sanskrit, sthitaprajna: wisdom that stands.

teach.h: THE TORTOISE DRAWS IN ITS LIMBS.
teach.b: Then a picture: like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, this person can draw the senses back from what pulls at them. And a few verses on, Krishna roots it deeper: the steady one rests with the mind set on him.
That's how many Hindus read it: steadiness isn't numbness; it's a self content in the self, anchored in God. Now a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: NOT AFRAID OF EVIL TIDINGS: PSALM 112.
teach.b: Psalm 112, scripture for Jews and Christians, describes the righteous person in the King James Version: "He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD."
Same shape: a heart the next piece of news doesn't knock over. And an honest difference.

The psalm's steady heart is fixed by trusting the LORD; it says nothing about drawing in the senses. The Gita's sage draws the senses in like the tortoise, content in the self, with the mind set on Krishna.
Two pictures of a steady heart, each on its own road. Neither needs the other to be wrong.

how: Hindus read Bhagavad Gita 2.54–72 as a portrait of the sthitaprajna, the person of steady wisdom, and some recite these verses in daily prayer; Jews and Christians pray Psalm 112, whose righteous one shall not be afraid of evil tidings.

o: a mind that has memorized all of the holy books
a mind that never changes any of its opinions
a mind not shaken by sorrow and not craving joy

games.q: the steady one: tap the pairs.

s: the Gita's steady sage feels nothing at all
free of clinging, fear and anger, but content in the self, not empty.
Psalm 112 says the righteous shall not be afraid of evil tidings
his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD.
the Gita and Psalm 112 reach steadiness the same way
the psalm by a heart fixed in trust; the Gita by senses drawn in and a mind set on Krishna.

games.q: your brother's first review at work is glowing, and he's floating. the next week a coworker trashes his project. what would steady wisdom do?
o: take both the same way: hear them, keep what's useful, stay on his feet.
trust only the glowing review, since it came first and from his boss.
stop caring about feedback altogether, so nothing can hurt him again.
games.why: the steady one isn't shaken by sorrow or carried off by joy; the senses come back in, like a tortoise's limbs.

practice: Pick one sound around you: a fan, traffic, a bird, the hum of a fridge. Let it rise and fall, louder and softer, and let your attention stay where it is, the way a fixed heart stays put while the news comes and goes.

wordCard.voice: Steady wisdom: the Gita's sthitaprajna, the one not shaken by sorrow and not craving joy, wisdom that stands.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 2.54–56: one whose wisdom stands firm.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: steady, not shaken by sorrow, not grabbing at joy. Two days into the Gita.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.54 (Arjuna asks how the one steady in wisdom speaks, sits and walks)
Bhagavad Gita 2.55–56 (content in the self by the self; not shaken by sorrow, not craving joy, free of passion, fear and anger)
Bhagavad Gita 2.58 (like a tortoise drawing in its limbs)
Bhagavad Gita 2.61 (the mind set on Krishna)
